topics.title: Interpreter & virtual environments
topics.summary: Keep each project isolated and make the interpreter explicit.
topics.bridge: Use your existing Windows setup. Docker and WSL are optional for this roadmap.
learn: Inspect the installed interpreter before changing anything.
Create a project .venv and run Python through its explicit path.
Keep .venv, secrets and generated files out of Git.
topics.exercise: Follow docs/setup-windows.md and print sys.executable from the project interpreter.
topics.gate: A fresh terminal runs the tests with the same interpreter, without changing PowerShell policy.
explanation: An environment isolates project dependencies, while the interpreter still has its own version and executable path. Confirm both before installing or upgrading packages.
On your Windows workflow, invoking .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly avoids needing to change activation policy. Keep the environment reproducible rather than copying it between machines.

topics.title: A diagnostic, not a restart
topics.summary: Use existing Python exposure as an advantage and verify it with a small task.
topics.bridge: Your SQL, Power Query, API and analytics experience gives you useful mental models.

Group four EGP transactions with a dict.
Record which topics need practice; all progress begins unmarked.
topics.exercise: Try exercises/foundations.py tasks 02, 03, 07 and 10 before watching the matching chapters.
topics.gate: Explain your solution and edge cases without copying a reference answer.
explanation: Use existing Python exposure as an advantage and verify it with a small task. Your SQL, Power Query, API and analytics experience gives you useful mental models.
Work through the practice with a tiny fixture, predict the result before running it, and record one boundary case. Use the exit check as evidence before moving on.

topics.title: Run a program
topics.summary: A program is an ordered set of instructions with observable output.
topics.bridge: A query returns rows; a script can coordinate several steps around those rows.
learn: Run a .py file and use print for visible output.
Distinguish source code from the interpreter that executes it.
Predict the output before running the program.
topics.exercise: Task 01: format a short pipeline completion message.
topics.gate: pipeline_message("landing", 4) returns "landing: 4 rows".
pitfalls: Returning a value and printing a value have different effects.
explanation: A program is an ordered set of instructions with observable output. A query returns rows; a script can coordinate several steps around those rows.
Work through the practice with a tiny fixture, predict the result before running it, and record one boundary case. Use the exit check as evidence before moving on.

topics.title: Variables, types & missing values
topics.summary: A name refers to an object; type determines the operations that object supports.
topics.bridge: Compare Python None with SQL NULL, and distinguish missingness from zero and an empty string.
learn: Use str, int, float, bool and None deliberately.
Convert text at input boundaries and inspect types.
Use integer minor units for these EGP exercises: 100 piastres = 1 EGP.
topics.exercise: Task 02: convert a decimal EGP string to integer piastres; reject fractions below one piastre.
topics.gate: "12.50" becomes 1250; "0.001" and "NaN" raise ValueError.
topics.code:
from decimal import Decimal
amount = Decimal("12.50")
piastres = int(amount * 100)
print(piastres)  # 1250; validate precision before int in real input code
pitfalls: bool("False") is True because the string is nonempty.
Binary floats are unsuitable for exact currency equality.
explanation: A name refers to an object; type determines the operations that object supports. Compare Python None with SQL NULL, and distinguish missingness from zero and an empty string.
Work through the practice with a tiny fixture, predict the result before running it, and record one boundary case. Use the exit check as evidence before moving on.

topics.title: Functions & explicit contracts
topics.summary: A function turns named inputs into a useful result with a clear contract.
topics.bridge: Think of a reusable Power Query function, but make data dependencies explicit.
learn: Separate input/output from transformation logic.
Use return values, parameters and small docstrings.
Specify valid inputs and the result unit.
topics.exercise: Task 03: calculate net revenue from gross and discount piastres.
topics.gate: net_revenue(10000, 1500) is 8500; a discount larger than gross is rejected.
pitfalls: A missing return produces None.
A function that mutates input may surprise its callers.
explanation: A function turns named inputs into a useful result with a clear contract. Think of a reusable Power Query function, but make data dependencies explicit.
Work through the practice with a tiny fixture, predict the result before running it, and record one boundary case. Use the exit check as evidence before moving on.

topics.title: Scope & side effects
topics.summary: Local names help a function behave predictably across calls.
topics.bridge: Avoid notebook state that makes a cell work only after an undocumented execution order.
learn: Trace local versus module names.
Pass configuration as a parameter.
Return a new value rather than modifying a shared dict accidentally.
topics.exercise: Task 04: add a category to a copied record without changing the original.
topics.gate: The original dict stays identical after classify_copy(record, "Food").
topics.code:
def classify_copy(record, category):
    result = dict(record)
    result["category"] = category
    return result
pitfalls: A shallow copy does not clone nested mutable values.
Mutable default arguments persist between calls.
explanation: Local names help a function behave predictably across calls. Avoid notebook state that makes a cell work only after an undocumented execution order.
Work through the practice with a tiny fixture, predict the result before running it, and record one boundary case. Use the exit check as evidence before moving on.

topics.title: Testing & debugging
topics.summary: A failing example is evidence you can narrow to a specific cause.

Keep assertions in tests; use explicit validation in application code.
topics.exercise: Task 05: fix mean_or_none so empty data is meaningful and zero is retained.
topics.gate: mean_or_none([]) is None; mean_or_none([0, 10]) is 5.
pitfalls: Do not use bare except to hide a failure.
assert can be disabled; it is not a production input-validation boundary.
explanation: A failing example is evidence you can narrow to a specific cause. Apply your troubleshooting habit: reproduce, inspect, change one thing, verify.

topics.title: Lists, slices & comprehensions

topics.exercise: Task 09: return the last n records without changing the input list.
topics.gate: latest([1, 2, 3], 2) is [2, 3]; n=0 returns []; negative n is invalid.
topics.code:
records = ["a", "b", "c"]
last_two = records[-2:]
print(last_two)
print(records)  # still intact
pitfalls: sort() changes the list and returns None.
items[-0:] returns the full list, not an empty list.
explanation: Sequences preserve order, including repeated values. A list can hold landing records, but it has no enforced table schema.

topics.title: Tests that catch a broken contract
topics.summary: Use examples and failure cases to protect meaningful behavior.
topics.bridge: Reconciliation checks become executable tests.

Use pytest later for fixtures and parametrization.

topics.exercise: Add a regression test for a defect you introduce in a working copy.
topics.gate: The test fails with the defect and passes after a targeted repair.
explanation: Choose tests that would catch a meaningful defect: a multiplied join, a lost zero, a conflicting key or a missing transaction rollback. A test that merely repeats the implementation’s calculation is weak evidence.
Keep network and clock behavior injectable. Use a temporary directory or database for I/O tests, then add a focused end-to-end fixture check that reconciles the exported result.

topics.title: DataFrames through a SQL lens
topics.summary: Use labeled tabular operations with explicit data types.
topics.bridge: Map WHERE → filtering, GROUP BY → groupby and SELECT → column projection.
learn: Inspect schema and null patterns before cleaning.
Use vectorized transformations and groupby.
Retain raw values when coercing dates or numbers.
topics.exercise: Reproduce ledger category totals with pandas and compare them with your pure-Python result.
topics.gate: Both outputs agree; explain how missing groups and numeric conversion are handled.
explanation: Inspect a sample, shape, dtypes and missingness before choosing a transformation. Keep a raw copy and a small typed contract so coercion failures remain visible.
When comparing pandas with SQL or Power Query, use identical row grain, null rules and grouping keys. Reconciliation is more useful than a screenshot of a successful notebook cell.

topics.title: Joins, nulls & grain
topics.summary: A join is a cardinality decision, not just a merge call.
topics.bridge: Use your star/galaxy modeling knowledge to prevent multiplied facts.
learn: Declare one row per entity before joining.
Use pandas merge(validate=...) and inspect unmatched keys.
Separate None, NaN, empty text and business-unknown values.
topics.exercise: Join a fact fixture to a duplicate dimension and make the validation fail.
topics.gate: No total changes silently; unmatched keys and duplicated keys have separate reports.
explanation: Declare the expected relationship before merging: one-to-one, many-to-one or many-to-many. Validate reference-key uniqueness before a join; counting rows only after multiplication can hide the reason a KPI changed.
Check unmatched keys in both directions and decide what an unknown dimension means. An inner join may discard legitimate facts, while filling every missing value with zero invents measurements.

topics.title: Build 02 · PixelFed quality CLI
topics.summary: Profile landing data and publish a quality report without rewriting source files.
topics.bridge: Extend your PixelFed contracts; social posts and profiles are not sales transactions.
learn: Inspect actual PixelFed filenames and grain before choosing checks.
Report missing IDs, invalid timestamps, duplicates and orphans.
Write a small JSON report and a quarantine file.
topics.exercise: Follow projects/02-pixelfed-quality.md using a copied sample, never the only landing copy.
topics.gate: Every rule has a test and an example; no indiscriminate fillna(0).
explanation: A quality rule needs a business meaning, severity and action. Profile a copied sample, then separate unacceptable identifiers from optional attributes whose unknown value may be valid.
Report the denominator for every percentage and preserve rejected records with reasons. Compare before/after quality using stable definitions; a smaller output is not automatically a cleaner one.

topics.title: Optional · a clean ML bridge
topics.summary: Carry reliable Python into model preparation and evaluation.
topics.bridge: Build on your ML direction after data contracts and reproducibility are solid.
learn: Split data before fitting preprocessing.

Choose an honest baseline and a metric aligned to the task.
topics.exercise: Write a leakage checklist and a small baseline experiment on an appropriately licensed dataset.
topics.gate: The held-out set never fits the imputer, encoder or scaler.
explanation: Fit preprocessing on training data and apply the learned transformation to held-out data. Splitting after imputing or scaling leaks information about the evaluation set.
Document the prediction target, observation time and availability of each feature. A feature that becomes known after the business decision can make an apparently strong model unusable.

topics.title: APIs, JSON & failure policies
topics.summary: Treat external data as an input that can be late, incomplete or unavailable.
topics.bridge: Use your networking and n8n experience to reason about timeouts and rate limits.
learn: Set an explicit timeout and validate response status and schema.
Use bounded retries only when appropriate; respect Retry-After.
Persist provider timestamp, fetch timestamp and provenance.
topics.exercise: Design an offline EUR/EGP quote fixture with provider_as_of and fetched_at; label it fixture data.
topics.gate: A stale or malformed quote is visible; a cached value is never labeled live.
explanation: Document timeout, schema, pagination, rate-limit and freshness behavior as separate parts of the API contract. HTTP 200 alone does not prove the payload is complete or current.
Retry only the failures and operations that justify it. Preserve the provider timestamp and fetch timestamp, and keep an offline fixture suite so provider outages do not break basic validation tests.

topics.title: SQL loading & idempotency
topics.summary: Loading twice should have a documented, stable outcome.
topics.bridge: Start with SQLite, then transfer the pattern to PostgreSQL or SQL Server.
learn: Parameterize SQL and use transactions.

topics.exercise: Run python -m projects.pipeline twice on the same fixture database.
topics.gate: Stored row count and total stay stable; conflicting duplicate records are rejected.
explanation: The same business key delivered twice must have an explicit policy: accept identical replay, reject a conflict, or apply a documented update rule. A random new identifier on every run prevents replay detection.
Verify database constraints and transaction behavior with deliberate failures. A successful second run should reconcile stored rows and totals, not merely exit without an exception.

topics.title: OOP, composition & data classes
topics.summary: Use objects to express a useful boundary, with functions for transformation logic.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Model a validated record with a dataclass and explicit units.
Pass an extractor into a pipeline instead of hard-coding its source.
Compare composition with inheritance using one concrete change request.
topics.exercise: Create an Order dataclass and a report service that accepts a fixture reader.
topics.gate: A second reader can be substituted without rewriting the aggregation; invalid input is rejected before creating the domain record.
topics.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    order_id: str
    total_piastres: int

order = Order("O001", 12550)
print(order.total_piastres)
pitfalls: frozen=True is not deep immutability for nested mutable objects.
Type annotations alone do not enforce a runtime schema.
explanation: A class is useful when related state and behavior form a stable concept. A dataclass reduces repetitive initialization and representation code, but it does not validate every input automatically. Keep boundary parsing separate from the trusted object.

Composition means a service receives the collaborator it needs: for example, a reader or a clock. This makes fixture tests possible without making HTTP calls. Inheritance is appropriate for a genuine substitutable relationship, not simply for sharing two helper methods.

topics.title: Iterators, generators & streaming
topics.summary: Process a sequence without requiring every record to be resident in memory.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Explain iterable versus iterator and one-pass consumption.
Yield parsed rows while the file context is open.
Use bounded batches and measure peak memory.
topics.exercise: Replace a fixture reader that returns list(reader) with a generator and compare peak memory on a larger synthetic file.
topics.gate: Both versions produce identical aggregates; the streaming version keeps peak memory bounded by the chosen batch and aggregation state.
pitfalls: An iterator may be exhausted after the first pass.
list(generator) materializes the records again.
explanation: A generator defers execution until the consumer asks for a value. That can reduce the input retained in memory, but an unbounded grouping dictionary can still grow with the number of distinct keys. Streaming describes the whole design, not merely the presence of yield.

Keep file ownership clear. Opening a file outside a generator and returning an iterator after closing that file creates a reader that cannot be used. Test early termination as well as complete consumption.

topics.title: Context managers & decorators
topics.summary: Make cleanup and cross-cutting behavior explicit without obscuring a function contract.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Use with and try/finally for deterministic cleanup.
Write one context manager that yields exactly once.
Preserve wrapped function metadata with functools.wraps.
topics.exercise: Create a timer context and a logging decorator for a fixture transformation. Test cleanup when the transformation raises.
topics.gate: The original error remains visible, cleanup always runs, and a decorated function keeps its name and docstring.
explanation: The with statement gives a resource an explicit lifetime. A generator-based context manager acquires the resource before yield and releases it in finally. Cleanup must not silently turn a failed operation into a successful result.

A decorator replaces a callable with another callable. Keep validation and business rules visible; a short timer or logging wrapper is easier to review than a stack of decorators that changes retry, transaction and exception behavior at once.

topics.title: Type hints, protocols & validation
topics.summary: Use static contracts to improve maintainability while validating external data at runtime.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Annotate collection element types and optional results.
Use Protocol to describe a small reader interface.
Distinguish a type checker from runtime parsing and validation.
topics.exercise: Type a reader returning Iterable[Order], then inject a fake reader in tests. Add a malformed JSON input test.
topics.gate: The fake satisfies the interface and the malformed payload is rejected independently of its annotations.
pitfalls: Use syntax supported by the selected interpreter; this repo baseline remains Python 3.11+.
explanation: Type hints describe expected values to editors and static tools. Python does not automatically reject a string passed into an int-annotated parameter. Validate untrusted CSV, JSON and environment values when they enter the application.

A protocol describes the operations a collaborator must support without requiring a shared implementation. Keep the interface narrow: one read method is easier to fake and reason about than a provider object exposing dozens of unrelated calls.

topics.title: Regex, Unicode & Arabic text
topics.summary: Treat encoding, normalization and business identifiers as separate decisions.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Read UTF-8 explicitly and retain original text.
Use raw-string patterns and fullmatch for full-field validation.
Explain Unicode digits versus an ASCII-only identifier contract.
topics.exercise: Validate ASCII order IDs, preserve Arabic category labels, and compare composed/decomposed forms without overwriting the raw value.
topics.gate: Arabic text round-trips; invalid identifiers fail; normalization is recorded and never silently merges distinct business keys.
topics.code:
import re
import unicodedata

raw = "عناية بالبشرة"
normalized = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", raw)
valid_id = re.fullmatch(r"O[0-9]{3}", "O001") is not None
print(normalized, valid_id)
explanation: Encoding converts bytes to text. Normalization changes the representation of some equivalent Unicode sequences. Neither operation decides whether two customer names represent the same person, and stripping Arabic characters is not a valid cleaning default.

Use a regular expression for a bounded structural rule, such as an order identifier. A pattern proving that text resembles an email or phone number cannot prove the person owns it. Keep that distinction clear when designing intake or data-quality rules.

topics.title: Packages & reproducible dependencies
topics.summary: Make the tool runnable from a clean environment with declared requirements.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Separate import package, distribution name and project directory.
Describe metadata and interpreter constraints in pyproject.toml.
Record a repeatable dependency set and test it in a clean environment.
topics.exercise: Package the quality CLI with a console entry point and run it after a clean install in a new virtual environment.
topics.gate: The command works outside the repository working directory and the setup documentation identifies the tested interpreter and dependencies.
explanation: A working notebook environment is not a reproducible installation contract. A project should declare what it imports and which interpreter it supports. Use a virtual environment so another project’s upgrades do not silently change this one.

Distinguish allowed dependency ranges from the exact set tested for an application release. Record the tool and versions used to reproduce that set. Build and install the package in a clean environment to catch accidental imports from the current directory.

topics.title: Time zones, money & measurement units
topics.summary: Make temporal and numeric meaning explicit before aggregation.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Store event and ingestion timestamps separately as aware UTC instants.
Convert to Africa/Cairo for display or a documented business date.
Use validated Decimal values or integer minor units with a rounding policy.
topics.exercise: Design a quote fixture contract with provider_as_of, fetched_at, rate precision, base and quote currency. Test an invalid date and stale quote.
topics.gate: A stale observation is not described as live; time conversion preserves the instant; amounts reconcile at the documented precision.
topics.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

instant = datetime(2026, 11, 1, 12, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
local = instant.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Africa/Cairo"))
print(instant.isoformat(), local.isoformat())
explanation: A timestamp without a time zone is ambiguous until a source contract supplies its meaning. The event time and the time your process fetched the event answer different questions. Keep both when freshness affects a downstream decision.

A currency amount and an exchange rate need different precision policies. EGP minor units work well for many expense amounts, but a forex rate may require more than two decimal places. Do not truncate a rate using the ledger’s amount parser. On Windows, install the first-party tzdata package in the project environment if IANA zone data is unavailable.

topics.title: Async I/O & bounded concurrency
topics.summary: Overlap waiting work while preserving deadlines and explicit failure policy.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Explain a coroutine, await, task and cancellation.
Limit concurrent requests and keep per-request timeouts.
Separate I/O waiting from CPU-bound transformation work.
topics.exercise: Use fake delayed fetches to compare sequential and bounded concurrent retrieval. Inject one timeout and check cancellation cleanup.
topics.gate: Concurrency never exceeds the limit; one timeout follows a documented policy; the test performs no live API calls.
topics.code:
import asyncio

async def fake_fetch(value):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return value

async def main():
    limit = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    async def bounded(value):
        async with limit:
            return await fake_fetch(value)
    print(await asyncio.gather(*(bounded(i) for i in range(4))))

asyncio.run(main())
explanation: Asyncio is most useful when a program spends time waiting for I/O. It does not make a CPU-heavy transformation faster merely because a function is declared async. Keep blocking work out of the event loop or choose a different execution model.

Bound concurrency to protect the provider and your own machine. A semaphore limits work in flight; a deadline limits how long a request may wait. Both differ from retries, which must also respect the endpoint’s replay safety and quota policy.

topics.title: Profiling, memory & measured optimization
topics.summary: Measure a bottleneck before changing a correct implementation.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Separate benchmarking from profiling.
Use cProfile and tracemalloc with a stated interpreter and workload.
Verify outputs and memory behavior after optimization.
topics.exercise: Profile the fixture pipeline and a scaled synthetic input; compare an eager reader with a bounded streaming design.
topics.gate: The report states input size, environment, elapsed time and peak allocation; outputs remain identical.
topics.code:
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
values = list(range(1000))
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
tracemalloc.stop()
print({"current_bytes": current, "peak_bytes": peak})
explanation: A profiler attributes execution cost to functions; a benchmark compares elapsed behavior under controlled conditions. Profiling adds overhead, so a profiler report is not automatically a fair benchmark between Python and native library code.

Measure the whole pipeline, including parsing, joins, serialization and database work. A faster line of code is not valuable if the dominant cost lies elsewhere. Keep the input and expected outputs fixed while changing one design choice.

topics.title: CSV, Parquet & schema evolution
topics.summary: Choose a storage format using types, access pattern and downstream compatibility.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Compare text CSV with typed columnar Parquet.
Read selected columns and inspect schema metadata.
Define compatible column changes, nullability and precision.
topics.exercise: Export a copied synthetic fixture to Parquet, reload selected columns and compare values, nulls and timestamp interpretation.
topics.gate: The round-trip report identifies every type conversion and the consumer can reproduce the expected row count and totals.
explanation: CSV is convenient for inspection and interchange, but it does not carry a universal typed schema. Parquet stores typed columnar data and can support reading only the columns needed by an analysis. Performance depends on the actual file layout and workload.

Schema evolution is a compatibility decision. Adding an optional field differs from changing a business key or reducing decimal precision. Keep a written schema contract and test an older consumer against the changed dataset before promoting it.

topics.title: Database transactions & connection lifetimes
topics.summary: Control the unit of work and distinguish a transaction from a connection.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Bind values as SQL parameters and keep identifiers controlled.
Demonstrate commit and rollback on a multi-row operation.
Close resources and define conflict handling before introducing concurrency.
topics.exercise: Port a fixture load to a chosen SQLAlchemy driver; fail the second write and prove the intended transaction boundary.
topics.gate: The rollback behavior matches the documented unit of work, duplicate delivery policy remains stable, and credentials stay outside source.
explanation: A connection is a communication resource; a transaction groups changes under a commit or rollback boundary. A context manager can make that boundary visible, but you must understand which context manages only the connection and which also manages the transaction.

Parameter binding protects values from being interpreted as SQL syntax. It does not turn an arbitrary user-provided table name into a safe identifier. Use a controlled identifier mapping and explicit database constraints for keys and uniqueness.

topics.title: Data apps with Streamlit, Plotly & Dash
topics.summary: Turn a tested dataset into an interface that communicates the right question.
topics.bridge: Apply this to your Python data tools, PixelFed quality work, n8n integrations or BI delivery when the project needs it.
learn: Choose one framework and learn its state/rerun or callback model.
Keep transformations testable outside the UI.
Show empty, stale and invalid-data states with accessible labels.
topics.exercise: Build a read-only quality dashboard from the synthetic CLI output. Show row counts, rejects, freshness and a filterable category chart.
topics.gate: The chart reconciles to the CLI output; empty filters have a clear state; a reviewer can identify the source and limitations.
explanation: Streamlit is useful for rapidly building Python-led data interfaces. Its execution and state behavior differ from a static Power BI report. Keep expensive data loading and transformations separated from the display and learn the cache/state rules before relying on them.

Plotly provides figures; Dash adds an application model with layouts and callbacks. Choose one small workflow first. Your existing Power BI skills transfer through metric definitions, filter behavior, accessible color and clear data provenance—not through copying every dashboard interaction unchanged.
